This is the index of all trainings and tutorials hosted in this KMS. Each training lives in its own folder under docs/trainings/ and gets its own section in the nav (mkdocs.yml).

Training Status File Naming Convention Available

To propose a new training, open a PR that adds a new folder here plus a nav entry in mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Consistent file naming makes files searchable, sortable, and predictable across teams and tools — a file's name alone should tell you what course it belongs to, which module and topic it covers, and what kind of content it is, without opening it.

Every course project at ESAIL has two sides:

  • SME-Content — a loosely-organized intake area for whatever the subject-matter expert (instructor) hands off. It isn't enforced; we just want the content.
  • eSAIL-Production — where ESAIL organizes, edits, and finalizes that content for Canvas, split into a working stage and a finished stage.

docs.title: Folder structure
docs.text:
26C-ENGR123-Abbrev_Title-SMELastname/
├── ENGR123-Course_Map-26C.xlsx
├── ENGR123-Recording_Schedule-26C.xlsx
├── ENGR123-Syllabus-26C.pdf
├── 01-SME-Content/
└── 02-eSAIL-Production/
    ├── Work/
    └── Final/
  • 01-SME-Content and 02-eSAIL-Production are numbered so they always sort in that order in a file browser, regardless of case. Work and Final aren't — with only the two of them, numbering doesn't buy much, so they're left simple.
  • SME-Content, Work, and Final have no required subfolders — they're left flat on purpose. See Why no subfolders below for why that works once you've seen how the naming convention works.
  • The Syllabus is a plain top-level file, not its own folder, alongside Course_Map-26C.xlsx and Recording_Schedule-26C.xlsx — all three track the whole project rather than living inside the SME or eSAIL side. Notice the term code 26C only ever leads a name on the project folder itself; on every file, it trails at the end instead — see Naming instructional objects.

docs.title: Naming the project folder
docs.text:
26C   -  ENGR123  -  Abbrev_Title  -  SMELastname
term     course      course title     instructor
Field Rule Example Term 2-digit year + a letter for the term: A = Spring, B = Summer, C = Fall 26C = Fall 2026 Course Subject + catalog number, no separator between them ENGR123, not ENGR-123 Course title An abbreviated course title, underscores between words, each word capitalized — this is the one place a title keeps its capitalization, since it's the course's own name, not a content descriptor Intro_Robotics Instructor The instructor's (the SME's) last name — the template placeholder says SMELastname specifically so it doesn't get mistaken for the eSAIL producer's name Smith

docs.title: The hyphen / underscore rule
docs.text:
Everywhere in this convention:

  • Hyphens (-) separate structured fields — term, course, module, topic, type.
  • Underscores (_) join words inside a single field — a descriptive title, or a multi-word category label.
  • Free-text content descriptors are lowercase (what a video or reading is about) — but category labels are capitalized (what kind of thing it is): the course title in the project folder name, type codes, and labels like Homework/Exam/Project/Part-A.

This is why a video file name reads ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops.mp4: hyphens mark where one field ends and the next begins, VID is capitalized because it names a category (the Canvas tool), and intro_to_loops is lowercase because it's describing content, not a category.

docs.title: Naming instructional objects
docs.text:
Every file name leads with the course code, then whatever locates it, then a 3-letter type code — not just a label, but the actual Canvas tool the content uses. Slides reuse VID (they're not a distinct Canvas tool, and it keeps them sorted next to their video), and UNK is a placeholder for when the tool hasn't been decided yet.

Code Canvas tool VID Video (also used for a video's accompanying slide deck) QIZ Quiz ASG Assignment — also covers Homework, Exam, and Project, since Canvas implements all of those as an Assignment under the hood DIS Discussion FIL Files / attachment tool — standalone distributable documents (readings, professor notes) PAG Pages — delivered as a Canvas page (readable in the browser) instead of a downloadable file UNK Tool not yet decided

There are two shapes, depending on whether the content belongs to one point in the course or to the course as a whole:

Topic-anchored — the locator leads, straight after the course code:

ENGR123 - M01 - T01 - VID - intro_to_loops.mp4
course     mod   topic type   descriptor

Absolute, course-wide — no Module/Topic, ever. These are numbered globally, so "Quiz 5" always means the same file no matter which module it came up in — the course map spreadsheet is the source of truth for exactly which module/topic something relates to, not the file name:

ENGR123 - QIZ - 01 . md
course    type  index

ENGR123 - ASG - Homework - 01 - differential_equations.md
course    type   label    index    descriptor

A label after the type code (Homework, Exam, Project) is optional, and only earns its place when the type code alone is ambiguous about which flavor this is — which is mostly ASG, since it covers several different kinds of submission. QIZ or DIS rarely need one. A redundant label (QIZ-Quiz-01) isn't wrong, just unnecessary.

Descriptors are always optional, but strongly recommended for VID.

docs.title: Why no subfolders
docs.text:
Because the type code is baked into the name, a flat folder is still easy to scan — nothing here needs a Videos/ or Quizzes/ folder to tell it apart from anything else in the same folder:

Work/
├── ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops.mp4
├── ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops.pptx
├── ENGR123-QIZ-01.md
├── ENGR123-DIS-05-ethics_in_ai.md
├── ENGR123-ASG-Homework-01-differential_equations.md
└── ENGR123-ASG-Exam-01.md

VID, QIZ, ASG, and DIS already say what each file is. Grouping by content type into subfolders is still a fine personal habit if it helps you browse, just not something the convention requires.

Multi-part content gets a -Part-A / -Part-B suffix — capitalized, since it's hierarchical/structural, not content. Use it for genuine sequential parts, or just to tell apart two items that would otherwise land on an identical name:

ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops-Part-A.mp4
ENGR123-ASG-Exam-01-Part-A.md

Exception — the Syllabus keeps the term code, as a trailing qualifier after the label (not a leading prefix like the project folder). That way, if a designer keeps several draft versions of the syllabus around while updating it for a new term, they all sort together under ENGR123-Syllabus-...:

ENGR123-Syllabus-26C.pdf

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: File name Meaning 26C-ENGR123-Abbrev_Title-Lastname The project folder for ENGR123, Fall 2026, taught by Lastname ENGR123-Course_Map-26C.xlsx The course map for that same project ENGR123-Syllabus-26C.pdf The syllabus for the Fall 2026 offering ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops.mp4 Module 1, Topic 1 video: "Intro to Loops" ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops.pptx That same video's slide deck — same name, different extension ENGR123-QIZ-01.md Quiz 1, course-wide — no module/topic code ENGR123-DIS-05-ethics_in_ai.md Discussion 5, course-wide: "Ethics in AI" ENGR123-ASG-Homework-01-differential_equations.md Assignment, labeled as homework since "Assignment" alone wouldn't tell you that: Homework 1 ENGR123-ASG-Exam-01.md An exam — implemented as an Assignment in Canvas, labeled Exam so a human can tell at a glance ENGR123-M01-T01-VID-intro_to_loops-Part-A.mp4 Part A of a multi-part video for Module 1, Topic 1

docs.title: Tracking content: the course map
docs.text: Every project keeps an ENGR123-Course_Map-26C.xlsx — a spreadsheet that inventories every piece of content (week, module, topic, title, file name) alongside an eSAIL production checklist (video editing, captions, ID check, SME review, Canvas upload, etc.), plus links to the source file and its Descript editing project. It carries a Legend tab with a full column-by-column reference, including this same naming convention.

docs.text: Take the 10-question quiz

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Ten questions covering the naming convention from the training page. Answer one at a time — if you miss one, that choice is eliminated and you try again, so you can't move on until you get it right. Finishing the quiz means you've got the whole convention down, no grading needed.

Questions are pulled from a bank and shuffled (wording, examples, and answer order), so what you see may differ from what someone else sees.

Once you finish, your email and a quick attempts-per-question summary are sent to esail-subscriptions@tamu.edu via Formspree.
